learningObjective: Distinguish SPMD-style compiler-driven parallelization (as in GSPMD) from manual multi-controller / MPMD approaches.

canonicalClaims.claim: In an SPMD compiler flow (e.g. GSPMD), every rank executes the same program that has been rewritten by the compiler from a single-device semantics-preserving graph, with sharding annotations propagated through operators and collectives inserted at reshard boundaries; the user does not manually write per-rank code.
conditions: The compiler has a partitioning pass that transforms operator implementations based on sharding specs.
Sharding annotations can be either user-provided (hints) or inferred (propagation).
nonImplications: Does not imply that SPMD forbids per-rank divergence at all: control-flow specialization is possible where needed, but the compiled artifact is a single program.
Does not imply that SPMD's generated collectives are always optimal; the partitioner's cost model may still miss reshard opportunities.

canonicalClaims.claim: Manual / MPMD-style parallelism requires the user to write separate programs (or explicit per-rank branches) that place ops on specific devices and issue collectives by hand.
conditions: The runtime dispatches distinct programs to different ranks or explicitly guards code paths per rank.
nonImplications: Does not imply that MPMD is inherently less efficient; it can express patterns SPMD partitioners struggle with (e.g. asymmetric pipelines).

misconceptions.claim: SPMD means every rank literally runs identical machine code including identical collective payload sizes at every step.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SPMD means a single-program model; per-rank differences in shard indices, buffer offsets and even control-flow specializations are permitted.

misconceptions.claim: GSPMD generates a program per device (MPMD), differing only in device IDs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: GSPMD produces one SPMD program run on all devices; per-device parameterization (mesh axis, rank id) is threaded through the same program.

misconceptions.claim: SPMD makes manual placement obsolete because the compiler always chooses the optimal sharding without any user hint.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The GSPMD paper explicitly relies on user-provided sharding annotations at least on some operators; the compiler propagates them but does not always synthesize them from scratch.

misconceptions.claim: MPMD is the same as pipeline parallelism; any pipeline-parallel scheme is by definition MPMD.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Pipeline parallelism can be expressed in either SPMD (one program with stage-specific branches driven by rank) or MPMD (separate stage programs); the two axes are distinct.
